newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Suspected N.Korea agents shoot defector near Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Suspected N.Korea agents shoot defector near Seoul.

text.p: Two suspected North Korean agents shot and seriously wounded a defector who is a relative of Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, police said on Sunday.

South Korean Prime Miniser Lee Soo-sung called an emergency meeting of security-related ministers to discuss the attack near Seoul, while police and military troops searched for the gunmen, officials said.

They said they suspected Pyongyang had ordered the men to attack Li Il-nam as a warning to both the Seoul government and to potential asylum-seekers after the defection of a high-level North Korean official now marooned in the South Korean mission in Beijing.
Tensions on the divided Korean peninsula have flared since Wednesday, when Hwang Jang-yop, a senior adviser to North Korean leader Kim, arrived by taxi at the diplomatic mission.

South Korea says Hwang is seeking asylum in the South, while a furious North Korea insists he was kidnapped. Hwang, ranked 24th in the Stalinist state's hierarchy, would be the most senior Pyongyang official to seek asylum in the South.
In Beijing, a North Korean official warned that Pyongyang would respond with force if the South compelled Hwang to go to Seoul.
Senior Superintendent Kim Choong-nam, who is heading a police probe into the shooting in South Korea late on Saturday, said Li was in critical condition.
"We have several clues for the case pointing to North Korea," he told Reuters.
He said Li, known in South Korea as Lee Han-yong, is the nephew of Sung Hye-rim, former wife of Kim Jong-il, who celebrated his 55th birthday on Sunday.

"Li told witnesses 'spy, spy' before he went unconscious," the police officer said. The gunmen used Belgian-made Browning pistols that have been frequently used by North Korean spies for attacks in the past, he added.
Li, 36, was shot outside his temporary home at Bundang, just south of Seoul, he said.
Officials at a nearby hospital said surgery on the defector could not remove a bullet in his head as it was too deeply lodged. Li remained unconscious.

Police said neighbour Park Chong-un briefly talked to Li as he lay outside his apartment and reported the shooting to police. Park and Nam Sang-hwa, who lived in the same apartment as Li, witnessed the attack through video monitoring devices from their homes.
Police believed the attackers used silencers, as neighbours heard no gunshots. An analysis of two used cartridges at the scene showed the weapons used were Browning pistols.
"I can sense that they were North Korean agents," said Lim Yong-son, a former first lieutenant in the Northern army, who defected to the South in 1995.
"They are warning that Seoul is not a safe place for betrayers," Lim said. "They must be from an execution squad."
The attack took place as China agonised over what to do with Hwang, who is a member of the powerful secretariat of the North's ruling Workers' (Communist) Party.

Allowing Hwang to go to Seoul, where he could be expected to reveal crucial secrets about the North, would offend Beijing's old communist comrades. Sending him back to Pyongyang would endanger China's ties with its new capitalist friend, which has already proved a valuable investor.

Hwang's apparent betrayal has caused a massive loss of face for a North Korean government already reeling from severe food shortages and economic disasters. Fearing retaliation, Seoul has ordered tighter security at all its overseas missions.
Police have been placed on alert across South Korea since the attack on Li, while military strike teams are on standby.
Li came to Seoul in 1982 from Europe where he had been studying. He is the first Northern defector to be shot in the South since the arch rivals fought the 1950-53 Korean War.
